name: Classic-Style Test 4
source: Original questions written for LSAT Trainer in the style and difficulty of recent LSATs. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: At the Brannock reservoir, swallows nesting under the high eaves of the old pump house fledge far more chicks per nest than do swallows nesting under the low footbridge nearby. Rats from the reservoir bank can easily climb to nests under the footbridge but cannot reach those under the pump-house eaves. Predation by rats, therefore, probably accounts for the difference.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Swallows at the pump house tend to lay their eggs earlier in the season than do swallows at the footbridge.
Rats are known to eat the eggs and nestlings of many kinds of birds, including several species of swallow.
Far more people walk past the footbridge nests each day than walk past the nests under the pump-house eaves.
Footbridge nests with rat guards last year fledged about as many chicks per nest as pump-house nests did.
Some swallows that nest at the pump house in one year go on to nest at the footbridge in the next.
questions.explanation: If footbridge nests protected from rats do as well as pump-house nests, the location itself isn’t the problem and rats are, which strongly supports the causal claim; that is (D). (B) is tempting but only shows rats can eat nestlings in general, not that they explain this difference. (A) and (C) offer alternative causes and so weaken the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rat predation probably explains why footbridge nests fledge fewer chicks than pump-house nests.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Footbridge nests fledge fewer chicks; rats can reach footbridge nests but not pump-house nests.

breakdown.analysis: Rats can reach the footbridge nests, sure. But lots of things differ between a low footbridge and high eaves: people, noise, timing, shade. How do we know it’s the rats? The best support is a test: take away the rats and see if the difference disappears. We need an answer that isolates rats as the cause or rules out the other differences.

choices.note: This hands you an alternative cause: earlier breeders might simply do better. That weakens the argument.
Tempting, because it shows rats can do the damage, even to swallows. But that’s general. It doesn’t show rats are what explains this particular gap between two sites.
Another alternative cause: human disturbance could be what hurts the footbridge nests. That weakens.
CORRECT. Same footbridge, rats blocked, and the nests do as well as the pump-house nests. That pins the difference on rats rather than on the location itself.
Irrelevant. Birds switching sites from year to year doesn’t tell you why one site fledges fewer chicks.

questions.stimulus:
Moreno: The warehouse workers’ union should accept the company’s contract offer. It raises wages 4 percent a year for three years, which is more than workers at any other warehouse in the region received in their most recent contracts.

Lyle: That raise is certainly generous. But the offer also lets the company require overtime on only one day’s notice, and workers with young children cannot arrange child care that quickly. The union should reject the offer unless that clause is removed.
questions.stem: Moreno and Lyle disagree over whether
choices: the offered wage increase is larger than the increases that other warehouse workers in the region recently received
workers with young children would have difficulty arranging child care on one day’s notice
the union should accept the company’s offer in its current form
the company would agree to remove the overtime clause from its offer
the size of the wage increase is the most important feature of any contract offer
questions.explanation: Moreno says the union should accept the offer as made, while Lyle says it should be rejected unless the overtime clause comes out, so they disagree about accepting the offer in its current form, (C). (A) is tempting, but Lyle concedes the raise is generous and never disputes the regional comparison. Moreno says nothing about child care (B) or about which feature matters most (E), and neither speaker predicts what the company will do (D).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Moreno: accept the offer, because the raise beats every other warehouse in the region; Lyle: the raise is generous, but reject the offer unless the short-notice overtime clause is removed.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Lyle grants Moreno’s point about the raise, so that’s not the fight. The fight is the bottom line: Moreno says accept the offer as it stands; Lyle says don’t, not with that clause in it. We need an answer about accepting the current offer.

choices.note: Tempting, since it’s Moreno’s main reason. But Lyle calls the raise ‘certainly generous’ and never challenges the comparison. No disagreement here.
Lyle says yes, but Moreno says nothing about child care. One speaker silent means no disagreement you can prove.
CORRECT. Moreno: accept it. Lyle: reject it unless the clause is removed, so not in its current form. Clear yes versus no.
Neither speaker predicts what the company will do. Lyle only says what the union should do if the clause stays.
Too strong, and nobody says it. Moreno relies on the raise but never claims it’s the most important feature of every contract.

questions.stimulus: Fitness columnist: Many trainers doubt that ice baths do athletes any good. But last month our magazine’s website invited readers to report whether taking ice baths after hard workouts reduced their muscle soreness. Of the 900 readers who responded, 85 percent said that the ice baths had helped. So most athletes who take ice baths after hard workouts get real relief from soreness.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the fitness columnist’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: takes for granted that readers who chose to report their experiences are representative of athletes in general
fails to consider that athletes may be able to reduce muscle soreness in ways other than taking ice baths
presumes, without providing justification, that athletes who feel less sore after workouts also perform better
takes for granted that because ice baths help most athletes, they help every athlete who takes them
criticizes ice baths on the grounds that some of the readers who responded did not benefit from them
questions.explanation: The 900 respondents are magazine readers who chose to write in, and readers who got relief are the ones most motivated to report it, so they may not represent athletes generally; (A) names this unwarranted presumption about a self-selected sample. (B) is tempting because it sounds like a missed alternative, but the argument says nothing about ice baths being the only remedy, so other remedies don’t matter. (D) describes an overgeneralization the columnist never makes; the conclusion says ‘most,’ not ‘every.’

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most athletes who take ice baths after hard workouts get real relief from soreness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 85 percent of the 900 website readers who chose to respond said ice baths helped.

breakdown.analysis: Who answers a ‘did ice baths help you?’ call on a fitness website? Mostly people who use ice baths and liked them. People who tried them, felt nothing, and moved on rarely bother to write in. That’s a self-selected sample, a classic sampling flaw; know it. It’s like a restaurant asking diners to post reviews and concluding most diners loved it because 85 percent of the reviews are glowing. We need an answer that says the sample picked itself and may not match athletes in general.

choices.note: CORRECT. The respondents volunteered, and people with good results are more likely to report them. The columnist simply takes for granted that this self-selected group matches athletes in general, and nothing supports that.
Irrelevant. The columnist never says ice baths are the only way to reduce soreness. Other remedies existing doesn’t touch whether ice baths work for most athletes.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Stretching reduces soreness, so stretching is the only thing athletes need to recover from hard workouts.

choices.note: The argument never mentions performance. It’s only about feeling less sore. This answer adds a link the columnist didn’t make.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Athletes who take ice baths feel less sore, so ice baths must make them run faster.

choices.note: Too strong a description. The conclusion says ‘most athletes,’ not every athlete. The columnist doesn’t overgeneralize to each individual.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Ice baths relieve soreness for most athletes, so they will certainly relieve yours.

choices.note: Opposite of what happens. The columnist praises ice baths; nothing in the argument criticizes them.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Fifteen percent of readers said ice baths didn’t help, so ice baths are worthless.

questions.stimulus: Many residents of Corbin believe that the sinkholes that keep opening around town are caused by blasting at the quarry that opened four years ago. But sinkholes have opened in the Corbin area at about the same rate for the past hundred years, both before and since the quarry opened, and they are just as common on the far side of the valley, well beyond the reach of the blasting. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choices: the blasting at the quarry has made sinkholes in Corbin more frequent than they would otherwise be
the quarry’s blasting is probably not what is causing Corbin’s sinkholes
sinkholes will stop opening in Corbin once the quarry closes for good
no human activity of any kind contributes to the formation of sinkholes
the bedrock beneath Corbin is dissolving faster now than it did a century ago
questions.explanation: The rate of sinkholes didn’t change when the quarry opened, and sinkholes are just as common where blasting can’t reach, so the evidence points away from the quarry as the cause; (B) completes the pushback. (A) repeats the popular view that the author is arguing against. (C) and (E) contradict the unchanged rate, and (D) is far broader than the evidence about one quarry.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Residents blame the quarry’s blasting for Corbin’s sinkholes; 2. sinkholes have opened at the same rate for a century, before and after the quarry opened; 3. they are just as common beyond the blasting’s reach.

breakdown.analysis: The word ‘But’ tells you the author is pushing back on the residents. If the quarry were the cause, you’d expect more sinkholes after it opened and more near it. Neither is true. So the blank should say the quarry probably isn’t the cause. Watch for the trap that repeats the popular view the author rejects.

choices.note: Tempting if you read fast, because it’s what the residents believe. But the author says ‘But’ and gives evidence against exactly this. It’s the view being rejected.
CORRECT. No change in the rate after the quarry opened and no difference outside the blasting zone: both facts point away from the quarry. ‘Probably’ fits the strength of the evidence.
Contradicts the evidence. Sinkholes opened at the same rate before the quarry existed, so there’s no reason to expect them to stop when it closes.
Too broad. The argument is about one quarry in one town. It says nothing about all human activity everywhere.
Contradicts the facts. The sinkhole rate is the same as a century ago, which gives no support for faster dissolving now.

questions.stimulus: Since the thermostat on Tavola Pizzeria’s only oven began malfunctioning, causing the oven to run considerably hotter than its setting, the restaurant has had to throw out many overcooked trays of roasted vegetables. Yet over the same period, customers have rated Tavola’s pizza crusts much more highly than before, even though the pizzas are baked in the same oven.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Customers who order pizza at Tavola seldom also order the roasted vegetables served there.
Since the malfunction began, Tavola’s cooks have been checking pizzas more often while they bake.
Tavola’s pizza recipe calls for an oven temperature well below the one at which crust crisps and browns best.
Tavola has raised the prices on its menu to cover the cost of the vegetables it has had to discard.
Many pizzerias use one oven for their pizzas and a separate oven for roasted dishes.
questions.explanation: If the recipe’s set temperature was too low for an ideal crust, an oven running hotter than its setting would push pizzas closer to the best temperature while overshooting for vegetables, so the defect helps the crust; that is (C). (B) is tempting, but checking more often could at most keep pizzas from burning; it doesn’t explain why crusts got better than before. (A), (D), and (E) don’t address why the same overheating improved the pizza.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The oven runs too hot and ruins vegetables, but pizzas from the same oven are now rated better than before.

breakdown.analysis: How can a broken oven make anything better? Only if the old temperature was wrong for pizza in the first place. Then ‘too hot’ for vegetables could be ‘just right’ for crust. It’s like a car whose speedometer reads low: a driver who always went too slow suddenly arrives on time. We need an answer showing the extra heat moves pizza toward its ideal, not away from it.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Who orders what doesn’t change what the oven does to the pizza.

Tempting, because it shows the cooks reacting to the problem. But extra checking could only prevent burned pizzas. It doesn’t explain why crusts are rated better than they were before the malfunction.
CORRECT. If the recipe’s temperature was below the best crust temperature, the extra heat fixes the crust while still overcooking the vegetables. The defect turns out to help.
Prices are a different dimension. This explains nothing about how the crusts improved.
Right topic, wrong group. Tavola uses one oven for both; what other pizzerias do is irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Urban planner: For most of the last century, Halvern’s downtown streets were laid out as one-way pairs designed to move commuter traffic quickly. Several nearby cities have recently converted such streets back to two-way traffic. Halvern should do the same with Pike and Orrin Streets. Most commuters now use the new bypass, so the one-way design no longer serves its original purpose, and two-way streets slow cars enough to make the sidewalks more inviting to shoppers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the urban planner’s argument?
choices: Halvern’s downtown streets were designed as one-way pairs in order to move commuter traffic quickly.
Several cities near Halvern have recently converted their one-way streets back to two-way traffic.
The one-way design of Halvern’s downtown streets no longer serves the purpose for which it was adopted.
Two-way streets slow cars enough to make the downtown sidewalks more inviting to shoppers.
Pike and Orrin Streets in Halvern ought to be converted to two-way traffic.
questions.explanation: Everything in the argument supports the recommendation that Halvern convert Pike and Orrin Streets to two-way traffic, which (E) restates. (C) is tempting because it is itself drawn from the fact that commuters use the bypass, but it is only a step toward the recommendation. (A) and (B) are background, and (D) is a supporting premise.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Halvern should convert Pike and Orrin Streets to two-way traffic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Commuters now use the bypass, so the one-way design no longer serves its purpose; two-way streets slow cars and make sidewalks more inviting to shoppers.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first two sentences are background: history and what other cities did. They don’t argue for anything; you can ignore them. The third sentence, ‘Halvern should do the same,’ is the recommendation, and the last sentence gives the reasons for it. Note the conclusion sits in the middle, not at the end. We need an answer that says Pike and Orrin should become two-way.

choices.note: Background. This is just history about why the streets were built one-way. It supports nothing.
Background again. Other cities’ choices set the scene, but the planner doesn’t even use them as evidence.

Tempting, because it follows from ‘most commuters now use the bypass,’ so it looks like a conclusion. But it’s an intermediate step: it exists to support the recommendation, so it isn’t the main point.
A premise. It’s one of the two reasons offered for converting the streets.
CORRECT. ‘Halvern should do the same with Pike and Orrin Streets’ is what every other claim is there to support.

questions.stimulus: Many older customers of Linden Street Pharmacy have trouble opening child-resistant medicine bottles, and some of them stop taking their medications as a result. Any customer can ask for easy-open caps instead, but few customers know this. So if the pharmacy posts signs at its counter announcing that easy-open caps are available on request, fewer of its older customers will stop taking their medications.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Most older customers who stop taking their medications do so mainly because they are unable to open the child-resistant bottles.
Some older customers who have trouble opening child-resistant bottles would notice the signs and ask for easy-open caps.
Easy-open caps cost the pharmacy no more than child-resistant caps do.
Older customers are more likely than younger customers to stop taking the medications that have been prescribed to them.
Signs at the counter are the most effective way to let customers know that easy-open caps are available on request.
questions.explanation: The plan works only if the signs actually reach some of the customers who struggle with the caps and lead them to ask for easy-open ones; negate (B) and the signs change nothing. (A) is tempting, but the argument needs only some customers to be helped, not a majority of those who stop. (E) is too strong: the signs need to work, not to be the best method.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Posting signs about easy-open caps will lead fewer older customers to stop taking their medications.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some older customers stop taking medications because they can’t open child-resistant bottles; easy-open caps are available on request; few customers know this.

breakdown.analysis: So what if there’s a sign? A sign only helps if someone who needs it sees it and acts on it. If every struggling customer ignored the sign or never asked, nothing would change. We need an answer that says at least some of the right customers will notice and ask. Assumption answers are often modest like this: ‘some,’ not ‘most.’

choices.note: Tempting, because it makes the caps sound like the main problem. But the argument only needs some customers to be helped. Negate it: even if most quit for other reasons, the ones who quit because of caps could still be helped. No damage.
choices.negation: Not most older customers who stop taking their medications do so mainly because they can’t open the bottles.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: none of the struggling customers would notice the signs and ask. Then the signs change nothing and the conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: No older customers who have trouble opening the bottles would notice the signs and ask for easy-open caps.

choices.note: Cost is a different dimension. Negate it: easy-open caps cost more. The signs could still keep customers on their medications. No damage.
choices.negation: Easy-open caps cost the pharmacy more than child-resistant caps do.

choices.note: An irrelevant comparison. Negate it: older customers are no more likely to stop than younger ones. The plan can still help the older ones who do stop. No damage.
choices.negation: Older customers are not more likely than younger customers to stop taking their medications.

choices.note: Too strong. The signs only have to work, not be the best option. Negate it: some other method is more effective. The signs could still help. No damage.
choices.negation: Signs at the counter are not the most effective way to let customers know about easy-open caps.

questions.stimulus: Marketing director at Pellbrook Press: Every novel on this year’s Coastal Booksellers bestseller list, which ranks novels by their sales in independent bookstores, was promoted with a tour of podcast interviews, and several of those novels were written by first-time authors. So if we arrange podcast tours for our debut novelists this spring, their novels will make that list.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the marketing director’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats a feature shared by all the bestselling novels as enough to make a novel a bestseller
draws a conclusion about all novels from a sample that consists only of the novels of debut authors
fails to consider that the Coastal Booksellers list might not accurately reflect how well novels actually sell
takes for granted that Pellbrook’s debut novelists would be willing and able to go on podcast tours this spring
presumes, without providing justification, that podcast tours are more effective than the other forms of book promotion that are available
questions.explanation: Knowing that every bestseller had a podcast tour shows at most that such a tour goes along with making the list, not that a tour guarantees it; many toured novels may have missed the list. (A) names this necessary-versus-sufficient confusion. (E) is tempting, but the director never compares podcasts with other promotion. (D) is merely possible and wouldn’t fix the argument even if the novelists were eager.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If Pellbrook gives its debut novelists podcast tours, their novels will make the bestseller list.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every novel on this year’s bestseller list had a podcast tour.

breakdown.analysis: Bestseller → podcast tour. The director flips it into podcast tour → bestseller. That’s confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient one. The detail about first-time authors doesn’t help: it still only describes novels that made the list. Maybe hundreds of novels had podcast tours and sank without a trace. It’s like saying every Olympic sprinter wears running shoes, so if I buy running shoes I’ll make the Olympics. We need an answer that says the argument treats something all the winners share as a guarantee of winning.

choices.note: CORRECT. All the bestsellers had tours, so a tour may be necessary, but the director treats it as sufficient. Lots of toured novels could have missed the list.
Backwards. The evidence is about bestselling novels in general, and the conclusion is about debut novels, not the other way around.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The three debut novels we published did well, so every novel we publish will do well.

choices.note: Merely possible. Nothing suggests the list is unreliable, and the flaw remains even if the list is perfect.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our book topped the list, so it outsold everything else, even though the list counts only a few stores.

choices.note: Merely possible, and beside the point. Even if every novelist happily toured, a tour still wouldn’t guarantee a bestseller.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We’ll book our authors on a twenty-city tour, so they will certainly do all twenty events.

choices.note: Tempting, because the director clearly loves podcasts. But there’s no comparison with other promotion anywhere. The argument would be just as flawed if podcasts were the best method.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Podcast tours sold some books last year, so they’re clearly the best way to promote any novel.

questions.stimulus: Last season Ridgefield High School required every player on its soccer teams to wear a newly designed padded headband during all of its games and practices, at a cost of about forty dollars per player. Over the season, team trainers recorded 30 percent fewer head injuries among the school’s soccer players than they had recorded the season before. So the headbands made Ridgefield’s soccer players safer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Players on the school’s basketball and lacrosse teams were not required to wear padded headbands last season.
Many of the soccer players complained throughout the season that the headbands were hot, heavy, and uncomfortable to wear.
In both seasons, the trainers recorded every head injury that occurred, no matter how minor.
Although fewer head injuries were recorded last season, more of them were serious concussions that sidelined players for weeks.
The headbands cost the school more than its athletic department had expected.
questions.explanation: The argument measures safety by the number of head injuries, but if the injuries that did happen were more often severe concussions, the players may not be safer at all; (D) introduces severity. (C) is the trap: it shows the counts were recorded consistently, which if anything helps the argument. (A), (B), and (E) are about other teams, comfort, and cost, none of which bears on safety.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The headbands made the soccer players safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After the headbands were required, trainers recorded 30 percent fewer head injuries.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of injuries really the measure of safety? Ten bumped heads can be less dangerous than three serious concussions. The argument counts injuries but ignores how bad they are. We need an answer that shows the injuries got worse even as the count went down. This is a measure mismatch: counts versus severity.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Basketball players aren’t part of the argument. Right topic, wrong group.
Comfort is a different dimension. Uncomfortable headbands can still prevent injuries.
Tempting, because it’s about how the injuries were counted. But it says the counting was consistent across both seasons, which supports the comparison. It doesn’t weaken anything.
CORRECT. Fewer injuries, but more serious concussions. If the injuries that happen are worse, the drop in the count doesn’t show the players were safer.
Cost is a different dimension. The headbands can be expensive and still make players safer.

questions.stimulus: Every worker at the Sayer foundry who took an unpaid leave of more than two weeks last year had that leave approved by the shop steward. Last year the steward approved such leaves only for workers with at least three years of seniority, and she approved none that included any days in December. Ilse, who has worked at the foundry for five years, took an unpaid leave of three weeks last year.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The steward approved Ilse’s leave in some month other than December.
Every worker with at least three years of seniority who requested a leave outside December last year had the leave approved.
Any worker who took an unpaid leave of two weeks or less last year did so without the steward’s approval.
None of the days of the unpaid leave that Ilse took last year fell in the month of December.
Ilse’s leave was the longest unpaid leave taken by any foundry worker last year.
questions.explanation: Ilse’s three-week leave was longer than two weeks, so the steward approved it, and the steward approved no such leave that included December days, so Ilse’s leave had none; that is (D). (A) is the trap: the rule limits which leaves were approved, not when the approval was given. (B) reverses a necessary condition into a sufficient one, and (C) and (E) go beyond the facts.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Unpaid leave over two weeks last year → approved by steward; 2. approved → at least three years’ seniority; 3. approved → no December days; 4. Ilse took a three-week unpaid leave last year.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it: Ilse’s leave was over two weeks → approved by the steward → no December days (and Ilse has the seniority, which we already knew). So we can prove her leave had no December days. Watch for answers that reverse a link or quietly change what the rule is about.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the December rule. But the rule is about leaves that include December days, not about when the steward signed off. She could have approved Ilse’s June leave in December.
This reverses the seniority rule. Seniority is necessary for approval, not a guarantee of it.
We don’t know this. The facts only cover leaves longer than two weeks. Shorter leaves might also need approval; we’re told nothing about them.
CORRECT. Over two weeks → approved → no December days. Ilse’s leave fits the chain, so none of it fell in December.
Unsupported ranking. Nothing tells us how long anyone else’s leave was.

questions.stimulus: Brisbury’s zoning policy is meant to let neighborhoods benefit directly from taller buildings. Under it, the city should grant a developer’s request to exceed a neighborhood’s height limit if the proposed building will include either affordable housing units or a new public park, provided that the proposal has first been presented at a public hearing held in that neighborhood.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the policy stated above?
choices: The Kell Tower proposal includes affordable housing units, and no hearing on it has been held yet, so the city should grant the developer’s request to exceed the height limit.
The Wilton proposal includes neither affordable units nor a public park, so the city should deny its request to exceed the height limit, even though it was presented at a hearing in its neighborhood.
The Lowe Street proposal was presented at a public hearing in its neighborhood, where residents spoke strongly in its favor, so the city should grant the request to exceed the height limit.

The Pardee proposal includes both affordable units and a public park but was presented only at a citywide hearing held downtown; nevertheless, the city should grant its request to exceed the height limit.
The Ardent Row proposal includes a new public park and was presented at a public hearing in its neighborhood, so the city should grant the request to exceed that neighborhood’s height limit.
questions.explanation: The policy says to grant the request when the building includes affordable units or a park and the proposal was presented at a hearing in that neighborhood; Ardent Row meets both conditions, (E). (B) is tempting, but the policy only says when to grant a request; it never says to deny one that falls short. (A) and (D) fail the neighborhood-hearing condition, and (C) fails the affordable-housing-or-park condition.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: (Affordable units OR new public park) AND presented at a hearing in that neighborhood → city should grant the height exception.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the project that meets both parts and gets the conclusion ‘grant.’

breakdown.analysis: Two conditions must both be met: (1) affordable housing or a park, either one is enough; (2) a hearing held in that neighborhood. Then the conclusion must be ‘grant.’ Note what the policy doesn’t say: nothing tells the city to deny a request. Traps will each satisfy only part of this.

choices.note: Condition 1 is met (affordable units), but there’s been no hearing. Condition 2 fails, so the policy doesn’t back granting.
Tempting, since Wilton really does fail condition 1. But the policy only tells you when to grant. Failing a sufficient condition doesn’t trigger a denial. That’s reversing the logic.
Hearing in the neighborhood, yes, but there’s no affordable housing or park. Residents’ enthusiasm isn’t one of the conditions.
It has both features, but the hearing was citywide and downtown, not in the neighborhood. The policy requires a hearing ‘held in that neighborhood.’
CORRECT. A park satisfies the ‘either/or’ condition, and the hearing was held in the neighborhood. Both conditions met, and the judgment is ‘grant.’

questions.stimulus: Preservationist: Councilor Brandt proposes protecting from demolition every building in Oakhurst that is more than fifty years old, on the grounds that age alone gives a building historic value. But under that standard, the cinder-block bus garage put up on Mercer Road in 1968 would merit the same protection as the town’s colonial courthouse. No one seriously regards that garage as a landmark. So age alone cannot be what gives a building historic value.
questions.stem: The claim that the bus garage would merit the same protection as the colonial courthouse plays which one of the following roles in the preservationist’s argument?
choices: It is a consequence of Councilor Brandt’s standard that the preservationist takes to be unacceptable.
It is the conclusion that the preservationist’s argument is designed to establish.
It is a premise that Councilor Brandt offers in support of the proposal.
It is offered as evidence that the courthouse has less historic value than is commonly believed.
It is a claim that the preservationist accepts and uses to show that some old buildings deserve protection.
questions.explanation: The preservationist derives the garage claim from Brandt’s age-only standard and then treats it as absurd, since no one considers the garage a landmark, in order to reject the standard; (A) describes this. (E) is the trap: the preservationist does not believe the garage deserves protection. (B) is wrong because the conclusion is that age alone can’t confer historic value, and (C) is wrong because Brandt never mentions the garage.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Age alone cannot be what gives a building historic value.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brandt’s age-only standard would protect a 1968 cinder-block bus garage just like the colonial courthouse; no one thinks the garage is a landmark.

breakdown.analysis: This is a ‘reduce it to absurdity’ move. The preservationist says: follow Brandt’s rule and you get a ridiculous result, the garage gets courthouse-level protection. The author doesn’t believe this. It’s the absurd result used to sink the rule. We need an answer that calls the claim an unacceptable consequence of Brandt’s standard.

choices.note: CORRECT. The garage claim follows from Brandt’s standard, and the preservationist finds it unacceptable. That’s what knocks out the standard.
The conclusion is the last sentence: age alone can’t give historic value. The garage claim supports that; it isn’t it.
Brandt never mentions the garage. The preservationist is the one who brings it up, against Brandt.
Nothing knocks the courthouse. The courthouse is the obvious landmark the garage is compared to.

Tempting, because the preservationist does state the claim. But the preservationist rejects it: ‘No one seriously regards that garage as a landmark.’ It’s used to sink the standard, not to protect old buildings.

questions.stimulus: In surveys, patients in the Calloway health system named cost more often than any other reason for failing to refill their blood-pressure prescriptions on time. Yet after Calloway made its most widely prescribed blood-pressure drug free to its patients, the proportion of patients taking that drug who failed to refill it on time did not decline at all.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why making the drug free did not reduce the proportion of late refills?
choices: Fewer than half of the patients who reported failing to refill on time named cost as their main reason for doing so.
Patients who refill their blood-pressure prescriptions on time suffer fewer strokes than patients who do not.
Most patients collect all their prescriptions in one pharmacy visit, which those short of money delay because their other drugs still cost money.
The free drug is as effective as the more expensive blood-pressure drugs that Calloway’s physicians sometimes prescribe.
Some patients who fail to refill their prescriptions on time do so simply because they lose track of when each of their refills is due.
questions.explanation: If patients collect all their prescriptions in one visit and short-of-money patients put off that whole visit because of the other, still-costly drugs, then the free drug gets refilled late anyway, so cost still drives the delay; that is (C). (A) and (E) are tempting because they point to reasons other than cost, but as long as cost was the most common reason, removing it should have reduced late refills at least somewhat, and the puzzle is that they didn’t decline at all.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Cost was the top reason for late refills, but making the drug free didn’t reduce late refills of it at all.

breakdown.analysis: If cost is the main reason people refill late, why didn’t ‘free’ help even a little? Maybe the cost that matters isn’t this drug’s price. If patients buy everything in one trip, and the trip is still expensive because of the other drugs, then making one drug free doesn’t change when they show up. We need an answer that shows cost still blocks the refill even though this drug is free.

choices.note: Tempting, because it shrinks the cost group. But cost was still the most common reason. Removing it should have reduced late refills somewhat, and they didn’t decline at all.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. It tells us why refilling on time matters, not why the free drug didn’t change behavior.

CORRECT. The refill is tied to one pharmacy trip, and that trip still costs money because of the other drugs. Patients short of cash postpone the whole trip, so the free drug is refilled late just as before. Cost still explains the delay.
Effectiveness is a different dimension. It doesn’t explain anything about refill timing.
Tempting, since forgetting is another cause. But ‘some’ forget doesn’t explain why the cost group, the biggest group, didn’t improve.

questions.stimulus: Publisher: Over four decades, our press built its reputation on accuracy, and we should not put that reputation at risk. Dr. Ames’s history of Harrow Lake is lively and well organized, but it makes many claims about local families that no one has checked against public records. So we should not publish the book in its current form.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the publisher’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Publishing a book that contains factual errors would put the press’s long-standing reputation for accuracy at risk.
The press should publish no book containing claims about local families unless those claims were checked against public records.
Most published histories of small communities contain at least some errors concerning local families.
Any book whose claims about local families have been checked against public records is accurate enough for the press to publish.
Dr. Ames did not consult any public records at all while writing his history of Harrow Lake.
questions.explanation: The book contains claims about local families that haven’t been checked against public records; if checking such claims is required before publishing, the book can’t be published as is, so (B) guarantees the conclusion. (D) is the trap: it gives the sufficient-condition version, telling us when a book may be published, which says nothing about an unchecked one. (A) fails because unchecked claims aren’t shown to be errors.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The press should not publish Ames’s book in its current form.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The press shouldn’t risk its reputation for accuracy; the book has many claims about local families that haven’t been checked against public records.

breakdown.analysis: Unchecked isn’t the same as wrong. So how do we get from ‘unchecked claims’ to ‘don’t publish’? The cleanest bridge makes checking a requirement: publish → claims checked. The book’s claims weren’t checked, so by the contrapositive: not checked → don’t publish. Chain: book has unchecked family claims → (rule) → should not publish. Watch for the sufficient version of this rule; it points the wrong way.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties into the reputation premise. But the book’s claims are unchecked, not shown to be false. Without knowing there are errors, this rule never kicks in.
CORRECT. Checking against public records is now a requirement for publication. The book fails it, so it shouldn’t be published as is.
‘Most histories’ having some errors makes errors likely, not certain, and still doesn’t say errors mean don’t publish. Not enough to force the conclusion.

Tempting, but it’s the wrong direction. It says when checked books may be published. It says nothing about what to do with an unchecked one. It’s the sufficient version of the needed necessary condition.
This explains why the claims are unchecked, which we already know. It still doesn’t tell us that unchecked means don’t publish.

questions.stimulus: Ten years ago, Wexley ranked third among the region’s twelve cities in the percentage of commuters who travel to work by bicycle, a figure the regional transit authority publishes each year. This year it ranked seventh. Clearly, then, the millions of dollars that Wexley spent building protected bike lanes during the past decade did not prevent bicycle commuting in Wexley from declining.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: fails to consider that protected bike lanes might provide benefits to the city other than an increase in bicycle commuting
overlooks the possibility that bicycle commuting in Wexley would have fallen even further had the new bike lanes not been built
presumes, without providing justification, that the region’s other cities spent less on bike lanes than Wexley spent
ignores the possibility that Wexley’s population grew more slowly over the decade than did the populations of the other cities
infers that Wexley’s own share of commuters who bike fell from a decline in how that share compares with other cities’ shares
questions.explanation: Falling from third to seventh shows only that more cities now have higher bike shares than Wexley; Wexley’s own share could have held steady or risen while others rose faster, and (E) names that relative-to-absolute slip. (B) is the dominant trap, but it describes a flaw the argument does not commit: the conclusion is only that the spending did not prevent a decline, which is true whenever a decline happened, even if things would have been worse without the lanes. (D) is irrelevant because the ranking is by percentage, which already adjusts for population.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bike-lane spending did not prevent bicycle commuting in Wexley from declining.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wexley fell from third to seventh of twelve cities in the percentage of commuters who bike.

breakdown.analysis: Did biking in Wexley actually go down? All we know is that its rank dropped, and rankings are relative. Picture it: Wexley goes from 8 percent to 10 percent while four other cities jump from 6 to 12. Wexley slides to seventh while its biking grows. Moving down a ranking isn’t an absolute decrease; that’s a classic slip, know it. We need an answer that says the argument reads a lower rank as a lower percentage. Most students pick (B), because ‘it would have been even worse without the lanes’ is the textbook objection to any before-and-after policy argument. It fails here because the conclusion is only that the lanes didn’t PREVENT a decline; if commuting fell at all, that’s true whether or not it would have fallen further. The right answer (E) hides behind abstract wording: ‘how that share compares with other cities’ shares’ is just the ranking.

choices.note: So? The argument never says the lanes were worthless. It says only that they didn’t stop a decline. Other benefits don’t touch that.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The new stadium didn’t raise tax revenue, so it did the city no good at all.

choices.note: Tempting. It’s the standard counterfactual objection, and it sounds like the right criticism of a policy argument. But read the conclusion: the spending ‘did not prevent’ a decline. If commuting fell, the lanes didn’t prevent the fall, even if things would have been worse without them. The argument doesn’t need to deny (B), so (B) isn’t its flaw.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Burglaries rose after we hired more officers, so hiring them made no difference to burglaries.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What other cities spent has nothing to do with whether Wexley’s own bike share fell.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our school’s test scores beat Lakeside’s, so our school must spend more per student.

choices.note: The ranking is by percentage of commuters, which already adjusts for population size. How fast the population grew explains nothing here.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our town has more car accidents than the village next door, so our drivers are worse.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘How that share compares with other cities’ shares’ is the ranking. The argument infers that Wexley’s own share fell from the fact that its rank fell, but the rank can drop while the share holds steady or rises.

questions.stimulus: Food writer: Some cooking instructors define a braise as any dish in which meat is cooked slowly in liquid in a covered pot. But consider a whole chicken poached gently in a covered pot of simmering stock. It satisfies this definition, yet no experienced cook would call it a braise. So the instructors’ definition is too broad.
questions.stem: The food writer’s argument proceeds by
choices: presenting a case to which the term being defined applies but that a proposed definition fails to include
presenting a case that meets a proposed definition but to which the term being defined does not apply
arguing that a definition is unreliable because those who proposed it lack relevant experience
showing that two competing definitions of a term classify the same dish in contradictory ways
inferring that because one dish cooked in liquid is not a braise, no dish cooked in liquid is a braise
questions.explanation: The poached chicken fits the instructors’ definition (meat, slow cooking, liquid, covered pot) but isn’t a braise, so the definition lets in something it should exclude, which is what (B) describes. (A) is the reverse: it describes showing a definition is too narrow, not too broad. (C) misreads the appeal to experienced cooks, which is about how the term is used, not about the instructors’ qualifications.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The instructors’ definition of a braise is too broad.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Poached chicken fits the definition, but no experienced cook would call it a braise.

breakdown.analysis: The move is a counterexample to a definition. Which kind? A definition can fail two ways: too broad (it lets in things that don’t belong) or too narrow (it leaves out things that do). Poached chicken fits the definition but isn’t a braise, so it gets in when it shouldn’t. That’s too broad. We need an answer that says ‘a case that meets the definition but isn’t the thing.’

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s also a counterexample to a definition. But it’s the too-narrow kind: a real braise the definition leaves out. Here the chicken is inside the definition and isn’t a braise.
choices.example: Example of this method: Some define a braise as meat cooked in wine. But short ribs braised in beer are clearly a braise, so the definition is too narrow.

choices.note: CORRECT. The poached chicken meets every part of the definition, yet it isn’t a braise. That’s exactly how you show a definition is too broad.
The writer never attacks the instructors’ experience. ‘No experienced cook would call it a braise’ is about how the word is used, not about the instructors.
choices.example: Example of this method: These instructors have never worked in a restaurant, so their definition of a braise can’t be trusted.

choices.note: Only one definition is on the table. The writer never offers a competing one.
choices.example: Example of this method: One chef defines a stew by its liquid and another by its cut of meat, and the two definitions disagree about chili.

choices.note: The writer doesn’t generalize from one dish. The point is that this one dish shows the definition fails, not that nothing cooked in liquid is a braise.
choices.example: Example of this method: Poached chicken isn’t a braise, so pot roast and short ribs aren’t either.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago, the town of Corvale planted a continuous row of shade trees along Bram Street, its main shopping street. Since then, the number of pedestrians using Bram Street on summer afternoons has risen by about a quarter. Evidently, the shade has made walking on Bram Street more appealing to people in hot weather.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, strengthens the argument EXCEPT:
choices: On nearby Tull Street, a similar shopping street with no shade trees, summer-afternoon pedestrian counts have not changed in three years.
Bram Street’s pedestrian counts on summer mornings and winter afternoons, when shade matters little, have not risen in three years.
Several new shops and cafés opened on Bram Street during the past three years, and they draw customers throughout the day.
Many people surveyed on Bram Street on hot afternoons said they chose it over nearby streets because it felt cooler.
Sidewalk temperatures on Bram Street on summer afternoons are now markedly lower than they were before the trees were planted.
questions.explanation: Four choices support the shade explanation: (A) supplies a tree-less control street that saw no rise, (B) confines the rise to times when shade matters, (D) gives walkers’ own reason, and (E) confirms the cooling mechanism. (C) instead offers a competing cause, new shops drawing foot traffic, so it weakens rather than strengthens. (E) is the most tempting wrong pick because it never mentions pedestrians, but showing the trees really cool the street makes the proposed mechanism more plausible.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The shade trees made walking on Bram Street more appealing in hot weather.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the trees were planted, summer-afternoon pedestrian counts on Bram Street rose by about a quarter.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: four answers strengthen, and the one you want either weakens or does nothing. So where’s the gap? Maybe Bram Street just got busier for other reasons: new businesses, more residents, a new bus stop. Strengtheners will rule out those other causes or confirm that the trees really cool the street. Mark each choice ‘S’ as you go and pick the one that doesn’t earn an S. Here, expect the odd one out to hand you another cause.

choices.note: Strengthens. A similar street without trees saw no change, so a town-wide rise in walking can’t explain Bram Street’s jump. That’s a control group.
Strengthens. Traffic rose only when shade matters. If something else had drawn people, mornings and winter afternoons would have risen too.
CORRECT. This is the odd one out. New shops drawing customers all day give a competing reason for more pedestrians, so it weakens the argument instead of strengthening it.
Strengthens. The walkers themselves say they pick Bram Street on hot afternoons because it’s cooler. Self-reports aren’t proof, but they support the shade explanation.

Tempting, because it doesn’t mention pedestrians at all. But the argument says shade made walking more appealing in the heat, and this confirms the trees actually cool the street. It supports the mechanism, so it strengthens.

questions.stimulus: Each spring the frogs of Harlan Pond begin their mating calls within two days of the same calendar date, even though the date on which the pond’s ice melts varies by as much as three weeks from one year to the next. Since the frogs’ start date does not track the melting of the ice, the frogs must be timing their calls by an internal clock rather than by any cue from their surroundings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Any frog population that times its mating calls by an internal clock starts calling within a few days of the same date every year.
Frogs in ponds where the ice melts at about the same time each year also begin calling on a consistent date each spring.
Nothing in the pond or its surroundings that the frogs are able to detect changes on nearly the same date each spring.
The temperature of the water in Harlan Pond plays no role at all in determining the date on which the frogs begin calling.
The date on which Harlan Pond’s ice melts has no influence on when the pond’s frogs lay their eggs.
questions.explanation: The argument rules out the ice as a cue and then concludes that no outside cue is involved. That leap requires that nothing detectable in the surroundings changes on a fixed date each year, because such a feature (day length, for instance) could produce a fixed calling date with no internal clock; that is (C). (D) is the dominant trap, but it is too strong: water temperature could nudge the date within the two-day window while a clock does the main timing. (A) reverses the reasoning, which runs from a fixed date to a clock, not from a clock to a fixed date.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The frogs time their calls by an internal clock, not by any cue from their surroundings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The frogs start calling within two days of the same date every year; the ice-melt date varies by up to three weeks, so the calls don’t track the ice.

breakdown.analysis: So the frogs ignore the ice. Does that mean they ignore everything outside them? Only if the ice was the only cue on offer. What about something in the surroundings that changes on the same date every year, like the length of the day? A cue like that would give a fixed calling date with no internal clock at all. The argument eliminated one outside cue and declared all of them gone. We need an answer that says there is no detectable outside cue running on a fixed yearly schedule. Most students pick (D), because temperature feels like exactly the outside cue the argument is ruling out. It fails because ‘no role at all’ is too strong: a clock could set the date while warm or cold water shifts it by a day, which even fits the two-day spread. The right answer (C) hides as a vague claim about ‘nothing in the surroundings,’ but it is the precondition the whole elimination step rests on.

choices.note: This reverses the reasoning. The argument goes from ‘same date every year’ to ‘internal clock,’ not from ‘clock’ to ‘same date.’ Negate it and some clock-timed frogs vary their dates. So? The Harlan Pond frogs don’t vary, and the argument says nothing about other populations.
choices.negation: Some frog populations that time their calls by an internal clock start calling on dates that vary widely from year to year.

choices.note: Interesting, but not required. Other ponds tell us nothing about which cue the Harlan Pond frogs use. Negating it doesn’t touch the argument.
choices.negation: In some ponds where the ice melts at about the same time each year, the frogs do not begin calling on a consistent date.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: something the frogs can detect, such as day length, changes on nearly the same date every spring. Then that cue could explain the fixed calling date, and the conclusion that no outside cue is involved collapses.
choices.negation: Something in the pond or its surroundings that the frogs can detect does change on nearly the same date each spring.

choices.note: Tempting. Temperature is the obvious outside cue, so ruling it out feels required. But this is too strong. Negate it: water temperature plays some role. The clock can still set the date while a warm or cold spell moves it by a day. The argument survives, so (D) isn’t required.
choices.negation: The temperature of the water in Harlan Pond plays some role in determining when the frogs begin calling.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Egg laying is a different event. The argument is only about when the frogs start calling.
choices.negation: The date on which the pond’s ice melts has some influence on when the frogs lay their eggs.

questions.stimulus: All cargo that arrives at the Port of Selmer from outside the country is opened and inspected by customs officers before it can leave the docks. The crates of machine parts unloaded at Pier 6 yesterday were opened and inspected by customs officers this morning. So the machine parts must have come from outside the country.
questions.stem: The pattern of questionable reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?
choices: A cake at Pella’s Café is labeled gluten-free only if it was baked on a Tuesday, after the ovens are cleaned. This torte was baked on a Tuesday, so it must be labeled gluten-free.
Only vessels that have been cleared by the harbor pilot may unload at the north wharf. The barge tied up there unloaded its cargo this morning, so it must have been cleared by the harbor pilot.
Every student who passed the final exam in Ms. Tran’s course received a certificate. Mira did not pass the final exam, so she must not have received a certificate either.
Most of the tenants who signed the petition attended last week’s building meeting. Hal attended that building meeting, so he probably signed the petition as well.
Every member of the choir sings at the spring festival, and everyone who sings at the festival receives a free ticket. So every member of the choir receives a free ticket.
questions.explanation: The argument treats a necessary condition as sufficient: cargo from abroad → inspected; these parts were inspected; so they came from abroad. (A) does the same once its ‘only if’ is read correctly: labeled gluten-free → baked on a Tuesday; the torte was baked on a Tuesday; so it is labeled gluten-free. (B) is the dominant trap because it reads in the same order as the original, but ‘only’ makes its rule unload → cleared, so its reasoning is valid. (C) negates the sufficient condition instead, and (D) uses ‘most’ and ‘probably.’

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The machine parts came from outside the country.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All cargo from abroad is inspected before it leaves the docks; the machine parts were inspected.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: From abroad → inspected. This was inspected. So it came from abroad. (Treats the necessary condition as sufficient.)

breakdown.analysis: Inspection is required for foreign cargo. Does that mean only foreign cargo gets inspected? No. Customs could open domestic crates too. It’s like saying: everyone who flies gets their bag scanned; my bag was scanned; so I flew. Maybe it was scanned at a courthouse. This is mistaking a necessary condition for a sufficient one; know it cold. Translate every answer into arrows before comparing. Most students pick (B), because it reads just like the original: a rule about a group, then an item that did the second thing, so it must have the first. But ‘Only cleared vessels may unload’ means unload → cleared, so the barge’s unloading guarantees it was cleared. (B) is valid; the original isn’t. The right answer (A) hides its flaw behind ‘only if’: labeled gluten-free → baked Tuesday, so a Tuesday torte isn’t guaranteed the label.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Labeled gluten-free only if baked on a Tuesday’ means label → Tuesday. The torte was baked on a Tuesday, and the argument concludes it’s labeled. That affirms the necessary condition, exactly as the original does.

Tempting. It reads in the same order as the original and is even set at a port. But translate it: ‘only cleared vessels may unload’ means unload → cleared. The barge unloaded, so it was cleared. That’s valid, and the original is flawed, so they don’t match.
A different error. Passed → certificate; Mira didn’t pass; so no certificate. That negates the sufficient condition rather than affirming the necessary one. Flawed, but not the same flaw.
Different quantifier and certainty. ‘Most’ plus ‘probably’ isn’t the all-plus-must pattern of the original. Whatever you think of this reasoning, it doesn’t match.
Valid chain: choir → sings → ticket. The original is flawed, so a valid argument can’t be the match.

questions.stimulus: Labor mediator: The Oriel Hotel’s management wants to require its housekeepers to wear location-tracking badges throughout their shifts, saying the data would help it schedule cleaning more efficiently. But the same scheduling gains could be achieved by having housekeepers log each room as they finish it, which would reveal far less about their movements. So the hotel should not adopt the badge requirement.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the labor mediator’s argument?
choices: Before adopting a practice that affects how employees do their jobs, an employer should first consult the employees who would be affected.
An employer should adopt any practice that makes its scheduling more efficient unless its employees formally object to the practice.
If a workplace practice would make operations more efficient without intruding on employees’ privacy, an employer should adopt it.
An employer should adopt a less intrusive practice in place of a more intrusive one only if the less intrusive practice also costs less.
An employer should not adopt a practice that intrudes on employees’ privacy if a less intrusive practice would serve the employer’s purpose equally well.
questions.explanation: The mediator rejects the badges because room logging would achieve the same scheduling gains with less intrusion; (E) says exactly that an intrusive practice shouldn’t be adopted when a less intrusive one serves the purpose equally well. (C) is tempting but only supports adopting the logging system; it says nothing about rejecting the badges. (A) and (B) turn on consultation and objections, which the argument never mentions, and (D) adds a cost condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The hotel should not adopt the badge requirement.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Room logging would give the same scheduling gains while revealing far less about housekeepers’ movements.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is ‘don’t adopt the badges.’ The reason is ‘a less intrusive option works just as well.’ So we need: if a less intrusive option serves the purpose equally well, don’t adopt the more intrusive one.

choices.note: Consultation never comes up. Even if the hotel consulted everyone, this principle wouldn’t say to reject the badges.
This would push toward adopting the badges unless someone objects, and no objection is mentioned. Wrong direction.
Tempting, because it praises the logging option. But it only says to adopt efficient, non-intrusive practices. It doesn’t tell you to reject the badges, which is the conclusion.
Cost is a different dimension, and the argument says nothing about cost. This adds a condition we can’t check.
CORRECT. Badges intrude; logging is less intrusive and serves the purpose equally well; so don’t adopt the badges. Every piece matches.

questions.stimulus: The mineral marlite forms only where molten volcanic rock comes into contact with seawater. Once exposed to air, marlite breaks down completely within two thousand years. Last year a landslide in the Corrin Highlands, a region far from any present-day coast, sheared away the face of a cliff, and the newly exposed rock was found to contain abundant marlite.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The marlite in the Corrin Highlands cliff must have formed sometime within the last two thousand years.
Any rock in the Corrin Highlands that has been exposed to air for several centuries contains no marlite.
Most of the marlite that has formed anywhere on Earth has since broken down completely as a result of exposure to air.
The rock containing the cliff’s marlite has never, since the marlite formed, been exposed to air for two thousand years or more.
Marlite is more abundant in the rock of the Corrin Highlands than in the rock found near present-day coasts.
questions.explanation: If the marlite-bearing rock had ever been exposed to air for two thousand years or more, its marlite would be gone; it still has abundant marlite, so it was never exposed that long, which is (D). (A) is the dominant trap: it starts the two-thousand-year clock when the marlite formed, but the clock runs only while the rock is exposed to air, so buried marlite could be far older. (B) misreads the time scale, since several centuries is less than two thousand years.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Marlite forms only where molten volcanic rock meets seawater; 2. once exposed to air, marlite breaks down completely within 2,000 years; 3. a landslide just exposed cliff rock in an inland region, and that rock has abundant marlite.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase fully, but fact 2 is a clock, and it only ticks while marlite is exposed to air. Exposed for 2,000+ years → no marlite left. Contrapositive: marlite still there → never exposed that long. The cliff rock still has plenty of marlite, so it was never exposed for 2,000 years. Most students pick (A), because they read the clock as running from the day the marlite formed: ‘it can’t last 2,000 years, so it must be young.’ It fails because breakdown starts only on exposure to air. Rock sealed inside a cliff could hold marlite millions of years old; the landslide only just started its clock. The right answer (D) is that contrapositive written as a ‘never,’ which is why it looks clumsy.

choices.note: Tempting. It’s the most natural reading of ‘two thousand years.’ But the clock runs only while marlite is exposed to air. Sealed inside the cliff, it could be millions of years old.
This misreads the time scale. ‘Within two thousand years’ allows marlite to survive several centuries of exposure, so rock exposed for a few hundred years could still contain some.
We don’t know this. Nothing says how much marlite has ever formed or how much of it has been exposed. One cliff can’t support a claim about the whole Earth.
CORRECT. Exposed for 2,000+ years → no marlite. This rock has abundant marlite, so since its marlite formed it has never been exposed that long.
No comparison is given. One cliff with abundant marlite says nothing about how common marlite is inland versus near the coast.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Adult male Tolland warblers have a white patch on the tail that is visible only when the tail is spread; females lack the patch entirely. Males spread their tails far more often during the three weeks before pairs form than at any other time of year. So the patch most likely serves to attract mates.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the ornithologist’s argument?
choices: Male Tolland warblers spread their tails at every time of year, including the months in which no pairs are forming.
The tail patch is slightly larger and brighter on older males than it is on younger males of the species.
Many songbird species have markings that are visible only when the birds spread their wings or tails in flight.
Females of a closely related warbler species prefer to pair with males whose white tail patches are larger than average.
Female Tolland warblers, which lack the patch, spread their tails about as often as males do in the weeks before pairs form.
questions.explanation: The ornithologist infers the patch’s purpose from when males spread their tails. (E) shows that females, which have no patch, spread their tails just as often at that time, so the seasonal tail-spreading serves some purpose other than showing the patch and the timing no longer points to mate attraction. (A) is the dominant trap, but the ornithologist already grants that males spread their tails at other times, only less often, so (A) conflicts with nothing in the argument. (D) supports the mate-attraction idea.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The males’ white tail patch most likely serves to attract mates.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The patch shows only when the tail is spread; females lack it; males spread their tails far more often in the three weeks before pairs form than at any other time.

breakdown.analysis: The whole argument is: it’s shown most during courtship season, so it’s for courtship. What would break that? Something showing that the tail-spreading in that season isn’t about the patch at all. If birds without the patch spread their tails just as much then, the spreading has some other job, and its timing tells us nothing about the patch. Most students pick (A): ‘males spread their tails all year, so it isn’t about mating.’ But reread the premise. Males spread far more often before pairing ‘than at any other time,’ which already allows spreading at other times. (A) attacks something the ornithologist conceded, so it doesn’t weaken. The right answer (E) looks off topic because it’s about the birds without the patch, and that’s exactly why it works.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds as if the patch isn’t tied to the mating season. But the premise already says males spread their tails at other times, just far less often. (A) is consistent with everything the ornithologist said.
So? A patch that grows with age fits a mate-attraction signal as well as any other function. If anything, it’s mild support.
Irrelevant. Other species’ markings don’t tell us what this patch is for or why the spreading peaks before pairing.
Opposite direction. If related females prefer bigger patches, that supports the idea that the patch attracts mates.

CORRECT. Females have no patch, yet they spread their tails just as often in the same weeks. So the seasonal spreading serves some purpose that has nothing to do with showing the patch, and the timing evidence loses its force.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: A prescription for a drug in the restricted category can be refilled without a new consultation only if the prescribing physician has signed a long-term-use authorization for that patient within the past year. Dr. Hale, who prescribes Velacor for Mr. Ruiz, signs such authorizations only during in-person examinations, and she has not examined Mr. Ruiz in person in more than two years. So Velacor must not be in the restricted category.
questions.stem: The pharmacist’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Mr. Ruiz’s prescription for Velacor was refilled last week, in full compliance with the rules, without a new consultation.
Dr. Hale has not signed a long-term-use authorization for Mr. Ruiz at any time within the past year.
Any drug for which a prescription can properly be refilled without a new consultation falls outside the restricted category.
If Dr. Hale had examined Mr. Ruiz in person within the past year, she would have signed an authorization for his Velacor.
Some of Dr. Hale’s other patients have had their prescriptions for Velacor refilled without a new consultation.
questions.explanation: The premises show that Mr. Ruiz has no authorization from the past year, so if Velacor were restricted, his prescription could not properly be refilled without a new consultation. (A) says it was properly refilled that way, so Velacor cannot be restricted. (C) is the dominant trap: it looks like the conditional bridge a sufficient-assumption answer usually supplies, but nothing establishes that a Velacor prescription can be refilled without a consultation, so its condition is never triggered. (B) only restates what the premises already establish.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Velacor is not in the restricted category.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Restricted drug refilled without a new consultation → prescriber signed an authorization within the past year; Hale signs only during in-person exams; she hasn’t examined Ruiz in over two years.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Hale hasn’t examined Ruiz in two years and signs only during exams → no authorization in the past year. Restricted AND refilled without consultation → authorization in the past year. Put together: if Velacor is restricted, Ruiz can’t be refilled without a consultation. So far the premises only say what WOULD happen if Velacor were restricted. To prove it isn’t, we need the other half: Ruiz did get a proper refill without a consultation. Refilled + no authorization → not restricted. Most students pick (C), because sufficient-assumption answers are usually ‘any X is Y’ bridges and (C) uses the right words. It fails because its trigger, a prescription that can be refilled without a consultation, is never shown for Velacor; the premises point the other way. The right answer (A) hides because it’s a plain fact, not a rule.

choices.note: CORRECT. A proper refill without a consultation, with no authorization from the past year, is impossible for a restricted drug. So Velacor isn’t restricted.
Already established. Hale signs only in person and hasn’t seen Ruiz in two years, so we know this. Repeating it adds nothing, and the conclusion still doesn’t follow.
Tempting. It looks like the bridge you expect. But it helps only if some Velacor prescription can properly be refilled without a consultation, and nothing says so. Its condition never gets triggered.
So? What Hale would have done after a hypothetical exam tells us nothing about which category Velacor is in.
Other patients may have recent authorizations from in-person exams. Their refills fit perfectly well with Velacor being restricted, so this proves nothing.

questions.stimulus: Literary agent: Admittedly, collections of previously published short stories rarely sell as well as novels do. But each of the twelve stories in Dara Vell’s new collection was praised by reviewers when it first appeared in a magazine over the past decade, and three of them won national awards. So reviewers will surely praise the collection as a whole.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the literary agent’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on the judgments of magazine reviewers who may have been biased in the author’s favor
treats the fact that the stories were published in magazines as evidence that they are of high literary quality
confuses the praise a book receives from reviewers with its success in the market for books
takes for granted that a work as a whole will be praised if each of its parts was
fails to consider that some of the stories in the collection may never have appeared in any magazine at all
questions.explanation: A collection of individually strong stories can still disappoint as a whole, for example if the stories feel repetitive side by side, so moving from ‘each story was praised’ to ‘the collection will be praised’ is a part-to-whole error, (D). (C) is tempting because of the concession about sales, but the agent sets sales aside and draws a conclusion only about reviewers’ praise. (E) contradicts the premise that each of the twelve stories appeared in a magazine.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Reviewers will surely praise Vell’s collection as a whole.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each of the collection’s twelve stories was praised when it first appeared in a magazine. (The agent concedes such collections rarely sell as well as novels.)

breakdown.analysis: So what if every story was praised on its own? A whole can be different from its parts. Twelve great stories might feel repetitive read back to back. It’s like saying every player on the team is an all-star, so the team will surely win the title. That’s the part-to-whole flaw (composition); it’s a classic, know it. The ‘admittedly’ sentence about sales is a side point the agent sets aside.

choices.note: Merely possible. Nothing suggests the reviewers were biased, and even unbiased praise of each story wouldn’t guarantee praise of the whole.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The reviewers loved her stories, and they’re all her old friends, so their praise proves the stories are excellent.

choices.note: The agent relies on reviewers’ praise, not on the mere fact of magazine publication. This describes evidence the argument doesn’t use.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Her stories ran in national magazines, so they must be excellent.

choices.note: Tempting, because the concession talks about sales. But the agent puts sales aside (‘Admittedly … But’) and concludes only about reviewers’ praise. No confusion between the two.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Critics adored the novel, so it will certainly be a bestseller.

choices.note: CORRECT. Praise for each story is taken for granted as a guarantee of praise for the collection. The parts having a quality doesn’t mean the whole has it.
Contradicts the premise. The agent says each of the twelve stories appeared in a magazine, so there’s nothing to overlook.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The stories I know about were praised, so every story in the book was praised, though some may be new.

questions.stimulus: Most of the recipes in Ilsa Ferro’s new cookbook, which is aimed at busy home cooks, require a stand mixer. Any recipe that requires a stand mixer is impractical for the many readers who cook in small apartment kitchens, where counter space is scarce. So most of the recipes in Ferro’s cookbook are impractical for those readers.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every apartment in the Larch Building faces west, and most west-facing apartments in the city are hard to rent in summer. So most apartments in the Larch Building are hard to rent in summer.
Every recipe in the cookbook that uses saffron is expensive to prepare, and most of the cookbook’s recipes are expensive to prepare. So most of the cookbook’s recipes use saffron.
Most of the trails in Dunn Park are steep, and most of the steep trails in the park are closed in winter. So most of the trails in Dunn Park are closed in winter.
Most of the trucks in the Kell fleet run on diesel, and every diesel truck must be inspected yearly. So every truck in the Kell fleet that must be inspected yearly runs on diesel.
Most apartments in the Larch Building will be hard to rent this summer, since most of them face west, and every west-facing apartment in the building is hard to rent in summer.
questions.explanation: The argument has a valid form: most A are B; every B is C; so most A are C.
