setup.text: All A are C; about half of B are C; some C are D; so some D are A and some D are B.

breakdown.analysis: Why is this bad? The funded documentaries could be ones that were neither nominated nor shown at Leland. Picture 100 documentaries this year: 5 nominated, 10 at Leland, and the 3 funded ones among the other 85. ‘Some C are D’ doesn’t say WHICH C’s. This is the overlap fallacy: two groups that both sit inside a bigger group needn’t overlap with a third slice of it. Most students pick (C), because its first two sentences are a near-copy of the original’s. It fails because its third premise says EVERY oil painting is insured, and ‘every’ guarantees the result, so (C) is valid. The right answer (B) hides by reordering: it starts with the ‘some’ statement and uses its own wording, but the pieces are identical.

choices.note: A different flaw: all chess members are math members; most math members are seniors; so most chess members are seniors. That’s the all-plus-most error, without the original’s two-part ‘some’ conclusion.

CORRECT. Some award winners (D) serve vegetarian dishes (C); all Pine Street restaurants (A) and about half of harbor restaurants (B) do too; so some award winners are A’s and some are B’s. Same overlap error, statements reordered.

Tempting. It opens exactly like the original. But its third premise is ‘every oil painting is insured,’ not ‘some.’ That makes the conclusion follow, so this argument is valid and can’t match a flawed one.
Only two groups and a ‘some … some’ chain: some volunteers are teachers, some teachers donate. A different error, missing the all / about-half structure.
A different flaw: it concludes that half the library is on the shortlist just because both groups contain English novels. There’s no third ‘some’ group and no two-part conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Westbury school district policy: A student may be excused from the physical education requirement only if a parent or guardian submits a written request for the exemption, and only if either the student has a physician’s note documenting a medical condition that makes participation unsafe or the student is a member of a school-sponsored sports team that practices at least four days a week.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the policy stated above?
choices: Lena’s mother submitted a written request, and Lena plays on the school’s volleyball team, which practices five days a week. So Lena must be excused from the physical education requirement.
Omar has a physician’s note documenting that his asthma makes participation unsafe, though no written request has been submitted for him. Since his need is documented, Omar may be excused.
Priya’s father submitted a written request, and Priya swims on a private club team that trains six days a week. So Priya may be excused from the physical education requirement.
Theo’s guardian submitted a written request, but Theo has no physician’s note, and his school’s cross-country team practices only three days a week. So Theo may not be excused.
Mira’s mother submitted a written request, and Mira has a physician’s note documenting a knee injury that makes participation unsafe. But she is on no school team, so she may not be excused.
questions.explanation: The policy lists only necessary conditions: a written request, plus either a physician’s note or a school team that practices at least four days a week. Theo has neither a note nor a qualifying team, so the policy rules out excusing him, which is (D). (A) is the dominant trap: Lena meets every condition, but conditions that are necessary don’t guarantee an exemption, so ‘must be excused’ doesn’t follow. (E) wrongly treats school-team membership as required even when there is a physician’s note.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Excused → (written request) AND (physician’s note OR school-sponsored team practicing 4+ days a week).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment the policy actually supports. Since the policy lists only requirements, it can prove that a student may NOT be excused (a requirement fails), but it can never prove that a student must or may be excused.

breakdown.analysis: Read ‘only if’ carefully. Both conditions are necessary, not sufficient. Contrapositive: no written request → not excused; no note AND no qualifying team → not excused. So a conforming judgment must deny an exemption to someone who fails a requirement. Check each student: Is there a request? Is there a note, or a school team with 4+ practice days? Most students pick (A), because Lena checks every box and ‘must be excused’ feels like the payoff. It fails because the policy never says meeting the requirements guarantees anything; necessary isn’t sufficient. The right answer (D) hides as a negative conclusion, which is the only kind this policy can deliver.

choices.note: Tempting. Lena meets every requirement. But the policy states only necessary conditions, so meeting them doesn’t make an exemption mandatory. ‘Must be excused’ doesn’t follow.
No written request → can’t be excused. The policy flatly rules Omar out, so ‘may be excused’ contradicts it.
Priya’s team is a private club, not school-sponsored, and she has no note. She fails the ‘or’ condition, so the policy rules her out.
CORRECT. Theo has a request, but no note and a team that practices only three days. He fails the ‘or’ condition, so by the contrapositive he may not be excused.
Mira has a request and a note, which satisfies the ‘or’ condition. The policy never requires team membership as well, so denying her doesn’t follow from the policy.

questions.stimulus: Literary historian: Late in her career, the novelist Edda Raske published three novels under the name ‘J. Halloran,’ and her authorship of them was not revealed until after her death. Critics at the time praised the Halloran novels far more warmly than the novels Raske was publishing under her own name in those same years. So Raske’s late reputation suffered from critics’ bias against her, not from any weakness in her writing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the literary historian’s argument depends?
choices: Most of the critics who reviewed Raske’s late novels disliked her personally and said as much in their published reviews.
Raske’s early novels were praised by the critics at least as warmly as the Halloran novels were later praised.
No other novelist of Raske’s time used an assumed name to avoid critics’ bias.
The Halloran novels sold more copies than the novels that Raske published under her own name during those years.
The Halloran novels were not substantially better written than the late novels Raske published under her own name.
questions.explanation: The historian credits the warmer praise for the Halloran novels to bias against Raske’s name, which requires ruling out the obvious alternative that the Halloran books were simply better; E does that, and negating it wrecks the argument. A is the attractive trap: personal dislike would support the historian, but the argument doesn’t need most critics to have disliked her or said so.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Raske’s late reputation suffered from critics’ bias against her, not from weak writing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Critics, not knowing Halloran was Raske, praised the Halloran novels far more than her own-name novels from the same years.

breakdown.analysis: Same author, same years, different name, warmer reviews. Bias, right? Only if the books were about equally good. What if the Halloran novels were just better books? Then the critics were judging fairly, and the warm reviews had nothing to do with the name. The argument needs to rule that out. We need a defender: the Halloran novels weren’t substantially better written than her own-name ones.

choices.note: Tempting, because it would support the bias story. But the argument doesn’t need most critics to dislike her, let alone say so in print. Bias can be quiet and partial.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the reviewing critics disliked her personally and said so.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How her early novels were received says nothing about why the late ones were judged differently.
choices.negation: Raske’s early novels were praised less warmly than the Halloran novels were.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether others used pen names has no bearing on why Raske’s two sets of books were reviewed differently.
choices.negation: Some other novelist of the time used an assumed name to avoid critics’ bias.

choices.note: Sales are a different dimension from critical praise. The argument is about reviews, not the market.
choices.negation: The Halloran novels did not sell more copies than her own-name novels.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the Halloran novels were substantially better written. Then the warmer praise is explained by quality, and the bias conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: The Halloran novels were substantially better written than her own-name late novels.
